utterance:
Here's what I've found. You have an acute strain of the muscles and soft tissues in your lower back — what we call acute mechanical low back pain. It's very common after lifting, and the spasm and tenderness I felt on the left side fit this exactly. Importantly, there's no sign of nerve damage: your leg strength, reflexes and feeling are all completely normal, and the pain isn't shooting down your leg.

I know you came in wanting a referral for an MRI, so let me explain my thinking. The Australian guidelines are very clear that for this type of back strain, scans are not recommended — and there are good reasons for that. Scans don't change how we treat this, they don't make you get better faster, and they often show wear-and-tear changes that are completely normal at your age and have nothing to do with your pain. Those incidental findings can cause a lot of unnecessary worry and sometimes lead to treatments you don't need. Your back should heal the same way whether we scan it or not. The situations where I would scan urgently are things like bladder or bowel problems, numbness around your bottom, weakness in the legs, fever, or a history of cancer — and you have none of those.

The vast majority of people with this are much better within two to four weeks, and often sooner. Does that make sense so far?
reply: That's a lot at once. I just want to know what the next steps are — I'm worried it's serious and I really want a scan.

utterance:
Fair enough — let me keep it simple. I understand it's worrying when you can barely move, but based on everything you've told me and my examination, this is a muscle strain, not something dangerous. There is no sign of nerve damage or any of the warning features we'd act on.

Here's the plan. First, keep moving — the worst thing for this is lying on the couch all day. Short walks, gentle movement, and getting up regularly will actually help it heal faster. Second, keep using heat on it. Third, for pain relief, I'll give you an anti-inflammatory tablet called ibuprofen, which works much better for this than paracetamol alone. Fourth, if it's not clearly improving over the next week or two, I'll refer you to a physiotherapist for hands-on treatment and exercises.

About the scan: I'm not going to order one today because it won't help you get better and isn't recommended for this. But if you're not improving over the next four to six weeks, or anything new develops, we'll reassess and can look at imaging then. How does that sound?
reply: I understand the plan, but I'm still worried it's serious and I really want a scan.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be

utterance:
Thanks for telling me — that's a really common worry, and it's worth talking through properly.

A 'slipped disc' only becomes a problem when it presses on a nerve. When that happens, you get very specific signs: pain shooting below the knee, numbness or pins and needles in the leg, actual weakness, or changes in the reflexes. I tested all of those on you today — your strength, reflexes and feeling are completely normal, and your pain stays in your back and buttock. So there's no sign of nerve pressure here.

The other thing worth knowing is that even when a disc does bulge, the vast majority settle on their own within weeks to a couple of months, without surgery. Surgery is the exception, not the rule. And here's the tricky part about scans: if I scanned 100 people your age with no back pain at all, a large number would show disc bulges and wear and tear. So a scan result often tells us very little about what's causing pain.

The honest answer is: a scan today wouldn't change your treatment, wouldn't speed your recovery, and could easily show an incidental finding that scares you without meaning anything. My strong recommendation is to treat this actively now, keep you moving, and review in one to two weeks. If things aren't improving, or any of those nerve signs appear, I'll scan you then without hesitation. Is that a fair deal?
reply: I guess I just want to be sure I'm not missing something. I'll try to keep moving and see how it goes.

awards.label: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily with food, short course

utterance:
Take one ibuprofen 400 mg tablet three times a day with food — taking it on an empty stomach can upset it, so always with a meal. If it causes stomach pain, heartburn or indigestion, stop it and let me know.

Now, the safety net — this is important, so please remember it. Go straight to the emergency department if you develop any of these: loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around your bottom or genitals, or weakness in either leg. Those are rare, but they'd be urgent. Otherwise, if the pain isn't clearly improving over the next week or two, or if it starts shooting down your leg, come back and see me — we'll reassess and reconsider scanning at that point.

In the meantime: stay active with short walks and gentle movement, avoid heavy lifting for now, keep up the heat pack, and don't spend all day lying down. Most people with exactly your presentation are much better within a couple of weeks. Do you have any questions before you go?
reply: No questions, thanks. I'll take the ibuprofen as directed and try to stay active.
